title: Three proofs that there are infinitely many primes

pages.title: Euclid
pages.intro: **Euclid, *Elements* IX.20 (about 300 BC).** Any finite list of primes leaves one out. Use **→** to step through the proof, and **PageDown** for the next proof.

nodes.title: Suppose
nodes.text: there are only finitely many primes, $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$.

nodes.title: Construct
nodes.detail: For the first six primes, $N = 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509$: $N$ need not be prime itself, only have a prime factor outside the list.

nodes.title: It is not on the list
nodes.text: If $q = p_i$, then $q$ divides both $N$ and $p_1 \cdots p_n$, so $q \mid N - p_1\cdots p_n = 1$. No prime divides $1$.

nodes.title: So
nodes.text: No finite list holds every prime: **there are infinitely many**.

steps.say: Start from any finite list of primes and multiply them all together, then add $1$.
Every integer greater than $1$ has a prime factor (its smallest divisor greater than $1$ is prime).
That prime cannot be on the list: it would divide the difference $N - p_1\cdots p_n = 1$.
The list was arbitrary, so no list is complete.

pages.title: Euler
pages.intro: **Euler (1737).** Unique factorization turns a sum over all integers into a product over the primes; the sum is infinite, so the product needs infinitely many factors. More: $\sum_p 1/p$ diverges.

nodes.title: Euler's product
nodes.detail: Expand each factor as a geometric series $\sum_k p^{-ks}$ and multiply out: each $n^{-s}$ appears exactly once, by unique factorization.

nodes.title: The sum is unbounded
nodes.text: As $s \to 1^+$, $\zeta(s) \ge \sum_{n \le M} n^{-s} \to \sum_{n \le M} \frac1n$, for every $M$; the harmonic series diverges, so $\zeta(s) \to \infty$.

nodes.title: If the primes were finite
nodes.text: the product would be finite too, tending to $\prod_p \frac{1}{1 - 1/p} < \infty$ as $s \to 1^+$.

nodes.title: And more
nodes.text: $$\log \zeta(s) = \sum_p \frac{1}{p^s} + O(1),$$ so $\sum_p \frac1p = \infty$: the primes are not even as sparse as the squares.
nodes.detail: Expand $\log \zeta(s) = \sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{p^{-ks}}{k}$. The terms with $k \ge 2$ add up to at most $\sum_p \frac{p^{-2s}}{1 - p^{-s}} \le 2 \sum_{n \ge 2} \frac{1}{n^2}$, bounded as $s \to 1^+$.

steps.say: Each integer is a product of primes in exactly one way, so the sum over integers factors as a product over primes.
The left side grows without bound as $s \to 1$; a finite product of factors each tending to $(1 - 1/p)^{-1}$ would not.
So the product has infinitely many factors.
Taking logarithms gives more than Euclid did: the sum of the reciprocals of the primes diverges.

pages.title: Fürstenberg
pages.intro: **Fürstenberg (1955), a proof by topology.** Arithmetic progressions make the integers a topological space in which finite unions of closed sets are closed, as always, and nonempty open sets are infinite.

nodes.title: The topology
nodes.text: Call $U \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ open when it is a union of progressions $$S(a, b) = \{a + nb : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}, \quad b \ge 1.$$
nodes.detail: The intersection of two progressions is empty or a progression (with modulus the lcm), so these sets are a topology.

nodes.title: Open sets are infinite
nodes.text: A nonempty open set contains some $S(a, b)$, which is infinite.

nodes.title: Progressions are closed
nodes.text: $$S(a, b) = \mathbb{Z} \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{b-1} S(a + i, b),$$ the complement of an open set.

nodes.title: The primes cover
nodes.text: Every integer except $\pm 1$ has a prime factor: $$\mathbb{Z} \setminus \{-1, 1\} = \bigcup_{p} S(0, p).$$

nodes.title: If the primes were finite
nodes.text: the union would be a finite union of closed sets: closed. Then $\{-1, 1\}$ would be open, and finite.

steps.say: Declare the arithmetic progressions, and their unions, open.
Two facts: nonempty open sets are infinite, and each progression is also closed, being the complement of the other residue classes mod $b$.
The multiples of the primes cover everything but $\pm 1$. With finitely many primes that cover is closed, so $\{-1, 1\}$ is open.
But a finite nonempty set is not open.
